A review22 and meta-analyses23,24 of studies comparing rate control with rhythm control found little difference between the two strategies in terms of symptom control or clinical events, and choice therefore depends on patient character- istics and preference.12-14,25 For elderly patients with min- imal symptoms rate control is generally the preferred op- tion, whereas younger patients or those who remain symptomatic despite rate control should be considered for rhythm control. Prophylaxis of atrial fibrillation may have a role in some situations. Although atrial fibrillation after cardiothoracic surgery is usually self-limiting, it may be associated with increased morbidity and mortality, and prophylaxis should be considered. Beta blockers, amiodarone, and sotalol are effective,13,14,26,27 and some benefit has also been reported with magnesium28,29 and corticosteroids.30 Use of statins31 or omega-3 fatty acids32 has also been investigated. For non-surgical patients, there is some evidence of a lower in- cidence of atrial fibrillation in patients taking drugs affect- ing the renin-angiotensin system,33 but the benefit of pro- phylactic use requires confirmation in controlled studies. Prevention of thromboembolic events, particularly ischaemic stroke, is a major aspect of atrial fibrillation management and has been the subject of several reviews34-38 as well as being addressed in the general re- views and guidelines quoted above. Patients are at risk both during cardioversion procedures and long-term, and should be given appropriate antithrombotic therapy. If atri- al fibrillation has been present for 48 hours or more it is generally recognised that there is a potential risk of caus- ing systemic embolisation once sinus rhythm is restored. In unstable patients who require immediate cardioversion, intravenous heparin should be given. In more stable pa- tients cardioversion should be delayed until the patient has received adequate anticoagulation with warfarin for 3 to 4 weeks, but if more rapid cardioversion is preferred, intra- venous heparin may be started, followed by transoesopha- geal echocardiography to exclude the presence of thrombi. Control of the ventricular rate as outlined above should be undertaken while the patient is waiting for cardioversion, and oral anticoagulants are usually continued for at least 4 weeks after a successful procedure.39 There is some evidence40 that subcutaneous low-molecular weight heparin may be an alternative to intravenous heparin fol- lowed by oral anticoagulants when transoesophageal echocardiography is used. Long-term prophylaxis is indicated in selected patients.
